newsitem.title: INDIA: Peaceful poll heralds new challenges for Punjab.
newsitem.headline: Peaceful poll heralds new challenges for Punjab.

text.p: A heavy voter turnout in India's Punjab state signalled a clear verdict against years of separatist violence, officials said on Saturday, but warned that the farming region now faced the challenge of peace.

More than 65 percent of Punjab's 15 million voters turned out on Friday in a dramatically peaceful election for the state legislature that is expected to thrust the pro-Sikh Akali Dal party into power.
The counting of votes is expected to start on Sunday and results could be announced the same evening, officials said.

The polls for the 117-seat assembly were the first in two decades not overshadowed by Sikh separatist violence, but officials said there were too many divisions within the state's political groups to ensure badly-needed stability.
"Peace was not the issue in the elections," said Tilak Raj Sarangal, district chief of Ludhiana, Punjab's business hub. "But it will be an issue for the new government."
Officials said former Punjab chief minister Prakash Singh Badal's Akali Dal party was sometimes seen in the past as sympathetic to Sikh militants' demands for a separate homeland called Khalistan.
Business leaders said the Dal's campaign of providing free electricity and water to farmers could be economically and politically disastrous.

"The state would lose 10 billion rupees ($280 million) in subsidies, if the Akalis implemented their plan for free perks to farmers," said Pitambar Datt Sharma, president of Punjab's Apex Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

"The government will then try to transfer the burden of the subsidy to industry," Sharma said. "That will not be prudent. Since the state's farmers are mainly Sikh and the Hindus are mostly urban businessmen, there could be communal ill will."

The Dal's poll alliance with India's main opposition group, the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), was seen as offering a chance to Punjab's two main communities -- Hindus and Sikhs -- to heal their mistrust, officials said.

"It is difficult to see how the Akali Dal will cut itself off from its pro-separatist past," one police official said. "It will not be easy for the BJP to sit back if the new government softens its attitude towards the militants."
Politicians said the Dal was too badly divided to last a full five-year term if it heads the new government.
"They will fall like a house of cards," said Kanshi Ram, head of the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), which wields considerable influence among Punjab's low-caste Hindus and Sikhs.
The BSP backed a hardline faction of the Akali Dal led by former police official turned politician Simranjit Singh Mann.
"It is never too difficult to divide the Akalis. There are so many ambitious leaders in the group with their own agendas," Ram told Reuters.
Punjab's ruling Congress party, led by the state's first woman chief minister Rajinder Kaur Bhattal, claims credit for the virtual weeding out of Sikh militancy from the region.
"We were the party that brought peace to this state," said the state's Minister for Technical Education Malkiat Singh Dakh. "If we lose, we could lose the initiative for peace."
Sikh separatist violence peaked after Indian troops were sent into the Golden Temple in Amritsar in 1984 to flush out militants holed up in the Sikhs' holiest shrine.

The showdown triggered a bloody spate of violence in the state. The then prime minister Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984, in what was believed to be a revenge killing for the army assault.
The state polls in 1992, which revived local democracy after more than a decade of separatist violence, were held in an atmosphere of fear and overbearing security. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
